clue.text: Severe operatic prince in endless stir

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
an endless word loses its final letter, so the synonym for stir is cut short

parts.note: to stir someone is to rouse them
Prince Igor is the title hero of Borodin's opera

explanation.surface: A stern opera prince is caught up in some commotion that never quite stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' drops the last letter of the synonym for stir; no word signals the insertion, the prince simply sits inside. Prince Igor is Borodin's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe strict, exacting standards or treatment, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Treatment favouring chums that sounds sexist?

definitions.meaning: the idiom for handing posts to one's friends, cronyism
a whimsical second reading: a phrase reserving work for males would sound like discrimination against women

explanation.surface: A remark that a policy of favouring one's pals sounds like it excludes women.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition takes the idiom literally: posts reserved for men, which would indeed be sexist.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names patronage or cronyism, giving positions to one's friends regardless of merit.

clue.text: Gulf that vessel floats on

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece sits on top of the second, as a boat floats on water

parts.note: a can is a container, a vessel
yon is an old or dialect word for that, as in yon hill

explanation.surface: A gulf identified as the one a ship floats on.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'floats on' sets the vessel above 'that', the way a boat rides on water; 'Gulf' looks like a sea but means a chasm.
explanation.definitionFit: A gulf can mean a deep chasm or ravine, which is what a canyon is.

clue.text: What is to some extent raw, rough, till beaten into shape

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the letters are found inside it

explanation.surface: Something raw and rough until it has been hammered into form, like metal on an anvil.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'raW ROUGH Till'; 'What is' only links the hidden letters to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrought iron is metal worked by hammering, so the word means shaped by beating.

clue.text: Agitation no end with affair that is oppressive

indicators.note: with no end the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a stir is a commotion or agitation
a fling is a brief love affair

explanation.surface: Endless upset together with a love affair makes for an oppressive atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' removes the final R of the agitation word; 'that is' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stifling heat or rules are suffocating and heavy, which is what oppressive describes.

clue.text: A hit tune, almost because somehow it connects to the listener

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are arranged afresh
almost the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A hit song somehow reaches whoever is listening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts TUNE to TUN; 'somehow' then rearranges A HIT TUN BECAUSE into the two words. 'the listener' is the ear, which this passage joins to the throat.
explanation.definitionFit: This canal links the middle ear to the throat, so it is connected to the organ of hearing.

clue.text: Fish not deprived of oxygen in stretch of water

parts.note: sole is a flatfish

indicators.note: deprived of means losing something, so a letter goes from the word

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A fish still has its oxygen while swimming in some water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deprived of' takes the O out of the word 'not'. The Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and the English mainland.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a named strait off southern England, an example of a stretch of sea.

clue.text: Greek character pinned by relatively insignificant monster …

indicators.note: something pinned by another is held fast within it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: minor means of lesser importance
tau is the Greek letter T

explanation.surface: A Greek person held down by a rather unimportant monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person, but it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The bull-headed creature of Cretan myth, kept in the labyrinth, is a legendary monster.

clue.text: … that character taken around fish

parts.note: refers back to the Greek letter of the previous clue, tau

indicators.note: turned around, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: got means obtained or taken

explanation.surface: Continuing from the monster: the same figure is captured around a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that character' points back to the Greek letter in the previous clue. The tautog is a wrasse of the American Atlantic coast.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a species of food fish of North America, so an example of a fish.

clue.text: It is a question about the old man's health

definitions.meaning: it is coy slang for sex, as in doing it

definitions.text: a question about the old man's health
definitions.meaning: taken literally, the phrase is an inquiry after one's dad

explanation.surface: Someone inquiring after your dad's wellbeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' looks like a mere pronoun, but it is the definition: coy slang for sex, of which this British phrase is a jokey euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses the phrase for sexual activity, which 'it' coyly denotes too.

clue.text: See 10
Expert leaving to enter wine store

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other, entering it

parts.note: a bin is a rack or store for bottles of wine
off means departing, as in I'm off

explanation.surface: A specialist heads off and goes into the cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: BOFFIN is British slang for a scientist or technical whizz.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal British word for a clever technical specialist, a synonym for an expert.

clue.text: See 2
Maybe helmet's protecting Irish copper in top operations

indicators.note: a covering protects what is inside it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a helmet is an example of hats, the plural; the apostrophe s is read as a plural
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A helmet protecting an Irish policeman during senior police operations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman, but it is the metal. 'top operations' are jobs done on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutting hair is work on the top of the head, so these are playfully operations on top.

clue.text: This rock not completely malleable? I allegedly use sand!

indicators.note: malleable things can be reshaped, so the letters are moulded anew
not the complete word, so its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Is this rock really pliable? A speaker claiming to make use of sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not completely' drops the K from ROCK; 'malleable?' reshapes THIS ROC. The bird is popularly said to bury its head in sand.
explanation.definitionFit: Folklore claims this large flightless bird hides its head in sand, which the bird itself is imagined saying.

clue.text: Firm given top grade, smart and doing well with little effort

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm
A is the highest exam grade
to smart is to sting with pain

explanation.surface: A company rated A, sharp and thriving without breaking a sweat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart' looks like an adjective for clever, but it is the verb meaning to hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: To coast is to progress easily without exertion, like freewheeling downhill.

clue.text: Most unexpectedly opposing everything offered by bookmaker

parts.note: against means in opposition to
all means everything
a bookmaker offers odds on outcomes

explanation.surface: A long shot that defies the bookie's prices and comes in anyway.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes success despite great improbability, which is surprising in the highest degree.

clue.text: Island noise interrupting end of wondrous song

indicators.note: the end of the word is its final letter
breaking into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in opera
din is loud noise

explanation.surface: A racket breaks into the close of a marvellous song on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the large Italian island in the Mediterranean, an example of an island.

clue.text: See 17
Books (hardback) in shopping centre store for a long time

indicators.note: one set of letters goes inside the other

parts.note: a mall is a shopping centre
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
HB is the abbreviation for hardback in book listings

explanation.surface: Hardback books in a shopping centre's shop sitting unsold for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'store' reads as a shop, but here it is the verb in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something in mothballs is to shelve it in long-term storage, so the verb means set aside for a long time.

clue.text: Obscure work — a strange hesitation to avoid it

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: the word avoids the hesitation, which therefore is taken out

parts.note: queer means odd or strange
er is the sound of hesitating

explanation.surface: An obscure piece of work, with an odd hesitancy that it tries to steer clear of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to avoid it' removes ER from QUEER to give QUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Opaque prose is hard to understand, the sense of obscure as unclear.

clue.text: Article in comic is only a rumour

indicators.note: the article goes inside the other word

parts.note: a card is a joker, a comic person
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece in a comic paper that turns out to be mere gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic' suggests a funny paper, but it is a person: a card is a wag.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is an unfounded story or false report, a kind of rumour.

clue.text: Islander certain to migrate, leaving island behind

indicators.note: letters that migrate move to new places, so they are rearranged
with behind, leaving something behind means dropping it, so a letter goes
completes the phrase leaving behind, which removes a letter

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for island on maps

explanation.surface: An islander is bound to emigrate, abandoning their island home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving island behind' drops the I from CERTAIN, and 'to migrate' rearranges CERTAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Crete, the Greek island, is an example of an islander.

clue.text: Underground accommodation teacher has to put up with in Scotland

parts.note: a rabbi is a Jewish teacher of the law
thole is a Scots verb for endure or put up with

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher living in a basement flat has to tolerate it while in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: THOLE is a Scottish and northern dialect word for endure.
explanation.definitionFit: The burrow a rabbit lives in is literally a home below ground.

clue.text: Labour's material electorate finally discarded

indicators.note: a discarded letter is thrown out of the word

parts.note: toile is a linen or cotton fabric

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: The Labour Party's literature, with the voters ultimately thrown aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' reads as the British political party, but the definition is the plain word for hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: Toil is hard, sustained work, a synonym for labour.

clue.text: See 6
One who wrote about pilgrim with no heart retreating

indicators.note: going backwards, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: nay means no
the nub is the heart or core of a matter

explanation.surface: A writer about a pilgrim who has lost heart and is backing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' only links: NAY and NUB, written backwards, give the name. John Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: John Bunyan's allegory follows the pilgrim Christian, so he is the writer about a pilgrim.

clue.text: A rum and I'd be exceptionally cordial

indicators.note: exceptionally suggests out of the ordinary, so the letters are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A rum and I'd be unusually friendly, says a drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cordial' reads as friendly, but here it is a sweet liqueur; DRAMBUIE is a Scotch whisky liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordial is a sweet, strong drink, and this honeyed whisky liqueur is an example.
